reddit_comments.text: Backtesting is essential but it's easy to fool yourself. A few things I learned the hard way: always use out-of-sample data (split your dataset into training and validation periods), account for slippage and fees (they eat into profits more than you think), and watch out for look-ahead bias. I run my backtests across different market regimes — bull, bear, and sideways — to make sure the strategy isn't just optimized for one condition. My current setup handles about 500+ trades in backtesting which gives a decent sample size for statistical significance.

After years of tweaking, I settled on a 6% stop-loss for crypto. Here's why: anything tighter gets stopped out by normal volatility (crypto moves 3-5% on a regular Tuesday), and anything wider means you're holding losers too long. Combined with 2% risk per trade and proper position sizing, it keeps drawdowns manageable. The key insight was that risk management isn't about avoiding losses — it's about making sure no single loss can derail your account.

I use a multi-indicator approach: EMA for trend direction, RSI for momentum/overbought-oversold conditions, MACD for confirmation, and Bollinger Bands for volatility context. No single indicator is reliable on its own — confluence is what gives you an edge. The real improvement came when I added multi-timeframe analysis: daily for the overall trend, 4H for entry zones. Eliminated a lot of false signals that way.

Drawdowns are inevitable — the question is whether your system recovers from them predictably. I track max drawdown, average drawdown duration, and recovery time. My bot's worst drawdown was around 18%, and it recovered within about 2 weeks. The mental shift that helped: treat drawdowns as the "cost of doing business" rather than failures. If your backtested max drawdown is 15%, expect to see 20% live. Always add a buffer.

I've been using Freqtrade for about a year and it's genuinely impressive for an open-source project. The strategy development workflow is solid: write your strategy in Python, backtest with historical data, paper trade, then go live. The community is active and the documentation is decent. Main downsides: the learning curve is steep if you're not comfortable with Python, and setting up proper data feeds takes some work. But once it's running, it's rock solid.

I paper traded for 3 months before going live, and I'd recommend at least 2 months minimum. Here's what paper trading revealed that backtesting didn't: order fill differences (slippage is real), API timeout handling, and how my strategy behaved during high-volatility news events. The psychological benefit is huge too — by the time I went live, I'd already seen drawdowns and recovery cycles, so I didn't panic at the first red day.

Win rate alone is misleading. I focus on three metrics: profit factor (total wins / total losses — anything above 1.5 is solid), SQN score (measures system quality over a large sample), and Sortino ratio (like Sharpe but only penalizes downside volatility). My current strategy runs about a 2.1 profit factor with a Sortino of 4.12, which I'm happy with. The SQN score of 3.8 tells me the system is genuinely robust rather than just lucky on a small sample.

Starting out with algo trading, I'd recommend this path: 1) Learn a framework (Freqtrade if Python, Hummingbot if you want market making). 2) Start with a simple strategy — even a basic EMA crossover. 3) Backtest extensively before adding complexity. 4) Paper trade for 2-3 months. 5) Start live with small capital. The biggest mistake I see is people jumping to complex ML strategies before understanding basic market mechanics. Simple strategies with good risk management beat complicated ones with poor risk management every time.

Sharpe ratio is useful but limited for crypto since returns aren't normally distributed. I prefer Sortino ratio because it only penalizes downside deviation — upside volatility is a feature, not a bug. My strategy's Sharpe is 2.34 and Sortino is 4.12, which tells me most of the volatility is on the upside. For context, anything above 2.0 Sharpe is considered excellent in traditional finance. In crypto you need higher because the baseline volatility is wild.

Multi-timeframe analysis was the single biggest improvement to my strategy. Before: trading on 1H charts only, getting chopped up by noise. After: using daily candles for trend direction, 4H for entry zones, 1H for fine-tuning. The logic is simple — don't take long entries when the daily trend is down, no matter how good the 1H setup looks. Eliminated about 30% of losing trades just with this filter. The tricky part is implementing it in code without look-ahead bias.

Funding rates and open interest are underused signals in algo trading. When funding is extremely positive (everyone's leveraged long), it often precedes a correction. I built a bot that factors this in as a filter — if funding rate exceeds a threshold, it tightens entries or avoids new longs entirely. It's not a standalone signal, but as a confirmation layer it's reduced false entries during euphoric tops. The data is freely available from most exchanges' APIs.

The main advantage of algo trading isn't speed — it's discipline. My bot doesn't revenge trade after a loss, doesn't move stop losses because it "feels" like the trade will recover, and doesn't skip entries because of fear. I backtested manually executing my own strategy for a month and found I deviated from the rules about 20% of the time. Those deviations cost me roughly 15% of potential profit. The algorithm follows the rules 100% of the time, 24/7.

Crypto's volatility is a double-edged sword for algo trading. On one hand, bigger moves = bigger opportunities. On the other, stop losses need to be wider, position sizes smaller, and your strategy needs to handle 10%+ daily swings without breaking. I use a 6% stop-loss which might seem wide in stocks but is actually conservative in crypto. The key is adapting your strategy to the asset class rather than applying stock market rules to a 24/7 market.

I tried 3Commas and Cornix before building my own system. They're fine for following signals, but you're dependent on someone else's strategy and paying monthly fees regardless of performance. Building my own bot with Freqtrade took more upfront effort but I control every parameter, can backtest properly, and don't pay subscription fees. The tradeoff is time investment — took about 3 months to get a strategy I was confident in. If you just want to follow signals, those platforms work. If you want to understand and control your trading, build your own.

Position sizing is where most beginners go wrong. They focus on entries and exits but size positions by gut feeling. I use a fixed percentage risk model: each trade risks 2% of current portfolio. Combined with a 6% stop-loss, this automatically calculates position size. As the portfolio grows, positions scale up. After drawdowns, they scale down — which is exactly what you want. Kelly criterion gives the mathematically optimal size but in practice I use half-Kelly because the real world has fatter tails than our models predict.

Overfitting is the silent killer of algo strategies. The telltale sign: your backtest shows 200%+ returns but live performance is flat or negative. What helped me: keep the number of optimizable parameters under 5, use walk-forward analysis instead of a single backtest window, and always hold out at least 30% of your data for validation. If the strategy doesn't perform at least 60-70% as well on unseen data as it does on training data, it's probably overfit. I also run Monte Carlo simulations to stress-test edge cases.

Exchange API reliability is something nobody warns you about until you're live. I've had orders fail silently, WebSocket connections drop during volatility spikes, and rate limits hit at the worst possible moment. My advice: always implement retry logic with exponential backoff, keep a local order state that reconciles with the exchange every few minutes, and have a kill switch that flattens all positions if the API is unreachable for more than X minutes. Redundancy matters more than speed for most retail algo traders.

Walk-forward analysis changed how I validate strategies. Instead of the classic train/test split, I use rolling windows: optimize on 6 months, validate on the next 2, then roll forward. If the strategy is consistently profitable across all walk-forward windows, it's likely robust. If it only works in 2 out of 5 windows, the edge is probably spurious. It's more work than a simple backtest but it's the closest thing to simulating how the strategy would have performed if you deployed it in real-time at each point in history.

Trading costs are the invisible tax that turns profitable backtests into losing live strategies. For crypto: maker fees are typically 0.02-0.1%, taker fees 0.04-0.1%, plus spread and slippage. On a strategy that trades 200 times a month, even 0.1% per trade adds up to 20% monthly drag. I always backtest with 1.5x the actual fee to account for slippage. It killed about a third of my strategies that looked great on paper. The survivors are the ones with genuine edge, not just fee-dependent arb.

Incorporating sentiment data into my algo was a game changer. Not as a primary signal, but as a filter. When the Fear & Greed Index is above 75, I reduce position sizes by 50% and tighten stops. When it's below 25, I increase size slightly and widen stops to give trades more room. The logic is simple: extreme greed = crowded longs = higher crash risk, extreme fear = capitulation = higher bounce probability. It's not perfect but it smoothed my equity curve significantly over a 12-month backtest.
